q: Cubic $x^3-px^2+qx-r=0$ (question text truncated in source; reconstructed from solution): (i) Suppose the roots are $a/k$, $a$, $ak$ (geometric progression). Show that $q/p=a$ and $q^3/p^3=r$. (ii) Show that the roots are in geometric progression if and only if $r\neq 0$ and $p^3r=q^3$. (iii) Show that the roots are in arithmetic progression if and only if $r=\frac{p}{3}\left(q-\frac{2p^2}{9}\right)$.
answer: (i) Matching coefficients with $(x-a/k)(x-a)(x-ak)$ gives $p=a(k^{-1}+1+k)$, $q=a^2(k^{-1}+1+k)$, $r=a^3$, so $q/p=a$ is a root and $q^3/p^3=r$. (ii) Substituting $x=q/p$ shows it is a root; the other two roots have product $q^2/p^2$, so they can be written $k^{-1}(q/p)$ and $k(q/p)$, giving geometric progression. Necessary and sufficient: $r\neq 0$ and $p^3r=q^3$. (iii) Roots $a-d$, $a$, $a+d$ give $p=3a$, $q=3a^2-d^2$, $r=a(a^2-d^2)$, so $r=\frac{p}{3}\left(q-\frac{2p^2}{9}\right)$. Converse: $p/3$ is a root, and the others are $p/3\pm d$. No conditions on $p$ or $r$ are needed for the arithmetic progression case.

q: (i) Let $f(x)=(1+x^2)e^x-k$, where $k$ is a given constant. Show that $f'(x)\geq 0$ and sketch the graph of $f(x)$ in the cases $k<0$, $0<k<1$ and $k>1$. Hence, or otherwise, show that the equation $(1+x^2)e^x-k=0$ has exactly one real root if $k>0$ and no real roots if $k\leq 0$. (ii) Determine the number of real roots of the equation $(e^x-1)-k\tan^{-1}x=0$ in the different cases that arise according to the value of the constant $k$.
answer: (i) $f'(x)=(1+x)^2e^x\geq 0$, with one stationary point at $x=-1$ (a point of inflection). $f(x)\to -k$ as $x\to-\infty$, $f(0)=1-k$, and $f(x)\to\infty$ as $x\to\infty$. Since $f$ is increasing with $0<f(x)<\infty$ when $k>0$, there is exactly one real root for $k>0$ and none for $k\leq 0$. (ii) Let $f(x)=(e^x-1)-k\tan^{-1}x$. Then $f(0)=0$, $f(x)\to k\pi/2-1$ as $x\to-\infty$, $f(x)\to\infty$ as $x\to\infty$, $f'(x)=e^x-k(1+x^2)^{-1}$, and $f'(0)=1-k$. Critical values are $k=0$, $2/\pi$, $1$. The equation has one root if $k\leq 2/\pi$ and two roots otherwise; at $k=1$ the root $x=0$ is a double root (counted as one or as two).

q: For each positive integer $n$, let $a_n=\frac{1}{n+1}+\frac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)}+\frac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)}+\cdots$ and $b_n=\frac{1}{n+1}+\frac{1}{(n+1)^2}+\frac{1}{(n+1)^3}+\cdots$. (i) Show that $b_n=1/n$. (ii) Deduce that $0<a_n<1/n$. (iii) Show that $a_n=n!e-[n!e]$, where $[x]$ is the integer part of $x$. (iv) Hence show that $e$ is irrational.
answer: (i) $b_n$ is a geometric series with first term and common ratio $\frac{1}{n+1}$, so $b_n=\frac{1}{n+1}\cdot\frac{1}{1-1/(n+1)}=\frac{1}{n}$. (ii) Each term of $a_n$ after the first is less than the corresponding term of $b_n$, so $a_n<b_n=1/n$, and $a_n>0$. (iii) $n!e=n!+n!+n!/2+\cdots+1+a_n$; all terms except $a_n$ are integers and $0<a_n<1$, so $[n!e]=n!e-a_n$. (iv) Suppose $e=k/m$ for integers $k,m$. Then $m!e$ is an integer, so $[m!e]=m!e$ and $a_m=0$, contradicting $a_m>0$.

q: To nine decimal places, $\log_{10}2=0.301029996$ and $\log_{10}3=0.477121255$. (i) Calculate $\log_{10}5$ and $\log_{10}6$ to three decimal places. By taking logs, or otherwise, show that $5\times10^{47}<3^{100}<6\times10^{47}$. Hence write down the first digit of $3^{100}$. (ii) Find the first digit of each of the following numbers: $2^{1000}$; $2^{10000}$; and $2^{100000}$.

For any number $x$, the largest integer less than or equal to $x$ is denoted by $[x]$. (i) Sketch the graph of $y=[x]$ for $0\leq x<5$ and evaluate $\int_0^5 [x]\,dx$. (ii) Sketch the graph of $y=[e^x]$ for $0\leq x<\ln n$, where $n$ is an integer, and show that $\int_0^{\ln n}[e^x]\,dx=n\ln n-\ln(n!)$. Hence show that $n!\geq n^n e^{1-n}$.
